extracted.intended_audience: educated readers, students of literature, and those interested in practical criticism and reading habits
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implicit evaluative criteria for reading, judging, and valuing authors and works (what to read, how to read, what to value in style, history, and poetry), drawn from Montaigne’s essay and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confession of ignorance as evidence of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: "The confession of ignorance is one of the finest and surest testimonies of judgment that I know.", i.e., acknowledging what one does not know demonstrates sound judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues humility about one's limits is better than pretending knowledge; admitting ignorance is preferable to the infirmity of judgment that cannot discern faults even when pointed out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value clearness of understanding and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer authors/readers who show 'clearness of understanding and judgment' and can distinguish 'the force and beauty of the discourse.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He says he admires anyone who can 'unplume' him by clearness — clear, persuasive exposition and the ability to reveal strength and beauty in argument or style is a mark of merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read for pleasure and self-knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: "I seek, in the reading of books, only to please myself by an honest diversion; or, if I study, 'tis for no other science than what treats of the knowledge of myself, and instructs me how to die and how to live well.", i.e., read primarily for personal pleasure and self-improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne places personal taste and practical self-knowledge above erudition for its own sake; choose readings that feed your curiosity and moral understanding rather than to accumulate learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pursue perfect knowledge at excessive cost
rubrics_metrics.description: "I could wish to have a more perfect knowledge of things, but I will not buy it so dear as it costs... there is nothing that I will cudgel my brains about; no, not even knowledge, of what value soever.", i.e., avoid obsessive or exhausting study for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a moderate, easy approach to learning; avoid squeezing oneself through laborious, joyless effort in pursuit of encyclopedic knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read with gaiety; avoid excessive persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: "I do nothing without gaiety; continuation and a too obstinate endeavour, darkens, stupefies, and tires my judgment.", i.e., intellectual pleasure sustains true understanding; overwork clouds judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a text resists immediate comprehension, withdraw and try later or take another work; persistent poring can dissipate sight and impede correct judgment (use fresh glances, repeated light passes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Switch books when not pleased or in mood
rubrics_metrics.description: "If one book do not please me, I take another; and I never meddle with any, but at such times as I am weary of doing nothing.", i.e., don't force a book when it doesn't suit you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne endorses reading opportunistically; do not punish yourself with texts that do not presently please or that require sustained endurance you lack.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer older/established works to novelty when fuller
rubrics_metrics.description: "I care not much for new ones, because the old seem fuller and stronger.", i.e., older works often offer greater depth and are worth preferring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He favors time-tested authors and suggests novelty is not inherently superior; judge books by substance rather than fashionable newness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer writings that present compact, self-contained pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: He praises Plutarch's minor works and Seneca's epistles as having 'discoursed in loose pieces, that do not require from me any trouble of reading long.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose works that allow stopping and starting without loss (epistles, short essays, minor works) if you dislike long continuous reading; format matters for accessibility and sustained use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with the main proposition; avoid needless preliminaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne criticizes Cicero's 'prefaces, definitions, divisions' and Aristotelian dispositions; "I would have a man begin with the main proposition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical readers, prefer directness and early delivery of 'good and solid reasons' rather than long preparatory flourishes; avoid rhetorical padding that delays the core point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor concise, shorter style over long cadences
rubrics_metrics.description: "For my part, I more approve of a shorter style, and that comes more roundly off."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise expression is praised; excessive long-period cadences (Cicero's mannerism) can be a fault. Economy of expression is a quality to value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style can outshine plot; elegance of diction is a virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The elegance and perfection of speaking can 'make us lose the appetite of his plot' — refined diction and grace can be central merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating poetry or fiction, value the allure of linguistic grace and sustained beauty; great style can compensate for weaker plot if it 'possesses the soul with his graces.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affectation and extravagant ornament in poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne admires ancients who 'avoided affectation and the hunting after... fantastic elevations' and prefers 'equal polish' and 'perpetual sweetness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique theatrical or overblown stylistic tricks; genuine polish and natural sweetness are superior to forced Petrarchan or fantastical flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic playwrights should rely on their own strength, not borrowed plots
rubrics_metrics.description: He criticizes modern comedians who 'take three or four plots of those of Plautus or Terence to make one of their own' — relying on others' matter shows diffidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A playwright's dependence on external stories to cover weak language or wit is a defect; prefer original material supported by strength of diction and invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good histories come from participants or eyewitnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: "The only good histories are those that have been written themselves who held command in the affairs whereof they write, or who participated in the conduct of them..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize histories authored by direct actors or eyewitnesses; such accounts better combine learning and authority, reducing certain kinds of error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in historians: confess and correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: He praises Froissart who, 'having committed an error, he is not ashamed to confess and correct it in the place where the finger has been laid.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A historian's willingness to acknowledge mistakes and print corrections is a positive trait; transparency in sources and errors increases trustworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historians should not select or abridge to impose their judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne warns middle-sort historians who 'chew our meat for us' and incline narratives to their own fancy; he demands they 'leave us something to judge of after them' and 'deliver it to us pure and entire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique historians who conceal, omit, or reshape facts to fit bias; prefer fuller presentation of material so readers can form their own judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not omit publicly known or 'ticklish' facts
rubrics_metrics.description: He condemns those who 'pass over in silence what all the world knows' (omitting important actions or names) as 'an inexcusable defect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Omitting widely-known facts to sanitize a narrative is unacceptable; completeness in reporting crucial incidents is required for trustworthy history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple eyewitness accounts and confrontation are ideal for historical truth
rubrics_metrics.description: He notes that when 'several eye-witnesses' write of the same subject, errors are likely slight, and advocates confronting witnesses and examining objections judicially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical truth is best supported by independent, corroborating eyewitness testimony and careful critical inquiry of discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer works that reveal the author's private humours and manners
rubrics_metrics.description: He 'delight[s] in reading the Epistles to Atticus... because I therein discover much of his own private humours' — personal writings reveal the author's true self.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For judging an author's character and natural opinions, value intimate genres (letters, memoirs) that expose private temper and habitual judgment more than public or performative works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep notes at end of books to record judgment and reading date
rubrics_metrics.description: Montaigne adopted a custom 'to note at the end of every book... the time when I made an end on't, and the judgment I had made of it' to aid his poor memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical reading habit: annotate completion date and a brief appraisal to preserve impressions and aid later recollection of why a book mattered or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish simple histories (raw reports) from judged narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: He distinguishes 'simple' historians (who record everything and leave judgment to readers) from 'more excellent' historians (who pick) and 'middle sort' (who bias): each has different value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the type of historian: raw compilations let readers decide; curated histories offer authorial judgment; middle-ground authors may introduce bias — choose according to your needs.
